newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU may allow shops to charge for payment by card.
newsitem.headline: EU may allow shops to charge for payment by card.

text.p: In a blow for the banking and payment card industries, the European Commission said on Monday it might allow shops to pass on credit and debit card fees to customers who pay with cards instead of cash.
Retailers, restaurants and other service providers have fought the banks for years over the right to share the card costs charged by banks with their clients.

The banks currently ban this on the grounds that consumers should not be penalised for using cards. But the Commission believes this hampers fair competition between different payment systems and weakens retailers' position with the banking system.
"The Commission has doubts about this rule; it would like it to disappear," a Commission spokesman told a news briefing.
Scrapping the rule would induce more transparent costs and allow retailers to negotiate better service fees with banks, the spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said.
He rejected any suggestion that the move would be bad for consumers.

The European consumer organisation BEUC is split on the issue. "BEUC does not have a position on the issue, the reason being that the views of national consumer organisations tend to differ depending on market traditions," BEUC spokeswoman Valery Thomson told Reuters.

Catherine Piana, adviser at Eurocommerce -- which represents European retailers and wholesalers -- said the row was about "a more equitable sharing of costs" between stores and card users. But it was not sure that consumers would end up paying a charge for using their cards.
In Belgium, where the non-discrimination rule has been made illegal for debit cards, retailers charge customers an extra five francs (14 cents) each time they pay with their card.

But in Britain, credit card holders are not charged even though the rule was suppressed in 1989. This may be due to British consumers being generally more organised and combative than in mainland Europe, industry sources said.
The rule is also illegal in Sweden and the Netherlands.
But Europay, which represents Eurocard, Mastercard and Eurocheque, argued that card holders had the right to know exactly how much they were paying for a service or goods and pay only that.
"It is not wise that merchants can go and surcharge whatever they want," a Europay spokesman told Reuters.

He argued that the commissions paid to banks were a fair price for the service they were getting. "A merchant pays a commission because he is buying a guarantee from the bank that the instrument he is accepting will be accepted by the bank," the spokesman said.
He added: "He is also paying for services rendered for managing payment systems and handling transactions."
Europay has 7,000 European member banks which have issued a total 145 million debit and credit cards.
Charges paid by stores and restaurants vary between less than one percent and five percent of sales. $1 = 35 Belgian francs
